# Introduction

The `jumps` package implements the method described in Maranzano and Pelagatti (2025), "A Hodrick-Prescott filter with automatically selected breaks", *Economic Modelling* 150, 107132, <doi:10.1016/j.econmod.2025.107132>. The terms *jumps* and *breaks* are used interchangeably in the package documentation. Indeed, in the initial version of the article, we used the term jumps, and one of the referees suggested that this term is generally devoted to the jump processes used in mathematical finance, while *breaks* is generally used in econometrics. We agreed with the referee and decided to use the term breaks in the article's final version. However, we decided to keep the term *jumps* in the package name and in the function names because we had already written most of it.

We introduced an innovation to the well-known Hodrick-Prescott filter (HPF) that allows for a small number of discontinuities in the otherwise smooth filter. The number, positions and magnitudes of these discontinuities, which we name *breaks* or *jumps*, are automatically estimated from the data. The method is based on the minimization of the sum of squared residuals of the HPF subject to a penalty on the number of breaks. The penalty is chosen by the user and can be set to zero, in which case the method reduces to the standard HPF. The technique is implemented in the `hpj` function, which is the main function of the package. The function `hpj` is a wrapper for other functions that implement various variations of the technique.

For efficiency, the package's computational engine is written in C++ through the Rcpp package. The engine implements the Kalman filter and smoother for the state-space form underlying the HPF. All formulae can be found in the article and in the vignette titled *Formulae*.

Users needing higher control over the estimation process can use the functions with names `hpfj*` and `auto_hpfj*`. However, the wrapper function `hpj` makes the process simpler and more stable. Indeed, good starting values are essential since the technique is based on a complex numerical optimisation. Inside the `hpj` function, we linearly transform the time series so that the starting values in the `hpfj*` functions are expected to work fine, and then we apply the anti-transform to all the results so that they refer to the original time series. The functions `hpfj*` and `auto_hpfj*` allow full control over the starting values and penalties.

While `hpfj*` and `auto_hpfj*` accept only time series stored in a numerical vector (any type of time series object is cast to numerical vector), the `hpj` function accepts all the main time series objects used in R (ts, zoo, xts, and timeSeries). All the time series generated by the function receive the same class and dates as the original time series.

# Basic usage

The function is called as

```         
hpj(y, maxsum = NULL, lambda = NULL, xreg = NULL, ic = c("bic", "hq", "aic", "aicc"), scl = 1000)
```
where `y` is the time series to be filtered, `maxsum` is inverse penalty, when zero no jumps are allowed, the larger `maxsum` the more and larger breaks are allowed, `lambda` is the smoothing parameter of the HPF, `xreg` is a matrix of regressors (we are still woring on this, so, at the moment it is not yet implemented), and `ic` is the information criterion used to select the penalty when `maxsum = NULL`. When `lambda = NULL`, the smoothing parameter is estimated by quasi maximum likelihood. The parameter `lambda` can be a positive number or one of the following strings (in parenthesis the value of the smoothing parameter corresponding to the string):
daily (110,930,628,906), weekly (45,697,600), monthly  (129,600), quarterly (1,600), annual  (6.25).

The function returns an object of class `hpj`, which is a list with the following slots:

- `y` the input time series;
- `maxsum` the maximum sum of additional standard deviations;
- `lambda` the smoothing constant of the HP filter;
- `pars` vector of estimated parameters (sigma_slope, sigma_noise, gamma);
- `hpj`: the time series of the HP filter with jumps;
- `hpj_std` the time series of the HP filter with jumps standard deviations;
- `breaks` vector of indices of the detected breaks;
- `sigmas` vector of additional standard deviations of the level disturbance;
- `xreg` matrix of regressors;
- `df` model's degrees of freedom;
- `loglik` value of the log-likelihood at maximum;
- `ic` vector of information criteria (aic, aicc, bic, hq);
- `opt` the output of the optimization function (nloptr);
- `call` the call to the function.

The methods `print` and `plot` are available for the `hpj` class. The `plot` method can be customised:
```
plot(x, prob = NULL, show_breaks = TRUE, main = "original + filter", use_ggplot = TRUE, ...)
```
where `x` is the object of class `hpj`, `prob` is the coverage of the confidence interval for the filter, which is not plotted when `prob = NULL`, `show_breaks` is a logical indicating whether to show the breaks in the plot, `main` is the title of the plot, `use_ggplot` is a logical indicating whether to use ggplot2, and `...` are additional arguments passed to the `plot` function when the standard plot is used (that is when `use_ggplot = FALSE`).

# Examples
## Simulated time series

```{r fig.width=5}
library(jumps)
set.seed(2025)
n <- 100

# simulated smooth trend
mu <- 100*cos(3*pi/n*(1:n)) - ((1:n) > 50)*n - c(rep(0, 50), 1:50)*10
# simulated time series
y <- mu + rnorm(n, sd = 20)

# HP filter with jumps with estimated lambda and fixed penalty (maxsum = 50)
hpj_sim <- hpj(y, maxsum = 50)

print(hpj_sim)

plot(hpj_sim)
plot(hpj_sim, prob = 0.95)
plot(hpj_sim, use_ggplot = FALSE)
```

## Nile time series

```{r fig.width=5}
# HP filter with jumps with estimated lambda and automatically selected penalty
hpj_nile <- hpj(Nile)

print(hpj_nile)

plot(hpj_nile, main = "Nile river flow")
plot(hpj_nile, prob = 0.95, main = "Nile river flow")
plot(hpj_nile, use_ggplot = FALSE, main = "Nile river flow")
```

## Employment in Italy

```{r warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, fig.width=5}
data("employed_IT")
y <- window(employed_IT[, "Y25.29"], start = c(2009, 1))
hpj_emp <- hpj(y, scl = "original")

print(hpj_emp)
plot(hpj_emp, main = "Millions of employed in Italy: age 25-29")
```


# Smoothing splines with jumps

Besides the HP filter, the package fits cubic smoothing splines that allow a
small number of discontinuities at unknown locations, following Pelagatti,
Maranzano and Gatto Ronchieri (2026).

The idea is to leave the classical roughness penalty untouched and instead
deform the domain over which it is computed. Every pair of consecutive
observations is granted a non-negative *domain warp* $\gamma_i \ge 0$, an amount
of fictitious domain length inserted between them, so that the latent spacing
becomes $\tau_i = \delta_i + \gamma_i$ with $\delta_i = x_{i+1} - x_i$. The
spline is fitted, and its roughness penalised, on this warped domain. Where the
signal is smooth, warping buys nothing and the optimal $\gamma_i$ is zero, so
the fit coincides with an ordinary smoothing spline; where the signal jumps, the
same vertical change can be spread over a longer warped interval, which lowers
its curvature cost dramatically. A budget $\sum_i \gamma_i \le M$ keeps the
warping concentrated on the few locations where a jump is actually present.

Four estimators are provided. `ssj_mle()` casts the model in state-space form
and estimates $(\sigma, \lambda, \boldsymbol{\gamma})$ by maximum likelihood
through the Kalman filter; `ssj_kfs()` does the same with $\lambda$ held fixed;
`ssj_atw()` is the fast alternating domain-warping algorithm, of complexity
$O(n \log n)$ per iteration; and `ssj_fix()` implements the earlier variant in
which the additional disturbance variances, rather than the spacings, are the
free parameters. The `auto_*` wrappers select the budget $M$ over a grid by
information criteria, EBIC by default.

## A simulated example

We use the test signal of Section 3 of the paper: a Bessel function of the first
kind carrying three discontinuities, at $x = 0.3$ (of size $+0.3$), $x = 0.4$
($-0.4$) and $x = 0.6$ ($-0.6$), observed at 100 random locations with Gaussian
noise.

```{r}
g1 <- function(x) {
  besselJ(20 * x, nu = 1) + x * (x >= 0.3 & x <= 0.4) - x * (x >= 0.6)
}
true_disc <- c(0.3, 0.4, 0.6)

set.seed(2026)
n <- 100
x <- sort(runif(n))
y <- g1(x) + rnorm(n, sd = 0.05)
```

We follow the two-step strategy of the paper's simulation study: a preliminary
`auto_ssj_mle()` fit supplies the smoothing parameter $\lambda$ by maximum
likelihood, and the fast alternating algorithm then uses it while EBIC selects
the warping budget. Note the two different values of `ebic_xi`: the likelihood
based estimators and the alternating algorithm compute the log-likelihood
differently, so the search penalty that delivers comparable sparsity is not the
same. Each function's default reflects that, and here we only override it for
the pilot.

```{r}
lambda_pilot <- auto_ssj_mle(y = y, x = x, ic = "ebic", ebic_xi = 0.1)$pars[["lambda"]]

fit_sim <- auto_ssj_atw(y = y, x = x, lambda = lambda_pilot, ic = "ebic")
fit_sim
```

The three discontinuities are recovered at
`r paste(round(ssj_breaks(fit_sim)$x, 3), collapse = ", ")`, against true
locations `r paste(true_disc, collapse = ", ")`, and the estimated jump sizes in
the table above are close to the true $+0.3$, $-0.4$ and $-0.6$. Recall that a
break is dated at the first observation belonging to the new regime, so the
reported location is the first sampled point after the discontinuity rather than
the discontinuity itself.

The `plot` method draws the fitted curve over the data and the estimated domain
warps below, which is where the jumps become visible: three spikes standing out
of an otherwise flat sequence.

```{r fig.width=6, fig.height=6}
plot(fit_sim, xlab = "x", ylab = "y")
```

Superimposing the true signal confirms that the fit is smooth between the
breaks and sharp at them.

```{r fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
plot(x, y, pch = 16, cex = 0.6, col = "grey55", xlab = "x", ylab = "y")
lines(x, g1(x), col = "grey20", lty = 2)
lines(fit_sim$x, fit_sim$smoothed_level, col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)
abline(v = ssj_breaks(fit_sim)$x, lty = 3, col = "firebrick")
legend("bottomleft", bty = "n", cex = 0.85,
       lty = c(2, 1), lwd = c(1, 2), col = c("grey20", "firebrick"),
       legend = c("true signal", "smoothing spline with jumps"))
```

# Application: electricity demand and temperature

The package ships the data used in the electricity demand versus temperature
application of `inst/scripts/load_temperature.R`. `load_temp` holds the full
hourly series (Northern-Italy load from the GME day-ahead market, Milan
temperature from the Open-Meteo archive, 2023-01-01 to 2025-09-30), while
`demand_temp` is the homogeneous analysis sample obtained from it: Tuesdays to
Thursdays only, non-vacation months, the central hours 10-15, and no extreme
loads or temperatures. Those filters strip out the weekday, holiday and
time-of-day effects that would otherwise confound the relationship of interest.

```{r}
data(demand_temp)
str(demand_temp)
```

Demand is a U-shaped function of temperature -- heating on the left, cooling on
the right -- but the interesting question is whether the curve is *smooth*.
Thermostat settings, air-conditioning switch-on thresholds and similar
behavioural rules suggest that it need not be.

Here we use the alternating algorithm `auto_ssj_atw()` rather than
`auto_ssj_mle()`, for two reasons. It is far faster: `ssj_mle()` estimates one
warping parameter per observation, which on these `r nrow(demand_temp)` points
takes minutes, whereas the alternating algorithm takes a fraction of a second.
And it collapses tied values of the covariate, which matters here because the
sample has only `r length(unique(demand_temp$Temperature))` distinct
temperatures: with ties left in place the budget can be spent warping the
interval *between two observations recorded at the same temperature*, which is
not identified. Since `ssj_atw()` needs $\lambda$ to be supplied, we pass the value obtained
from a preliminary `auto_ssj_mle()` fit -- the pilot strategy used in the
paper. That pilot must itself be run on the tie-averaged data, for the reason
just given: fitted on the raw observations it returns $\lambda = 154.5$, on the
averaged ones $\lambda = 254.3$.

```{r}
fit <- auto_ssj_atw(y = demand_temp$Load, x = demand_temp$Temperature,
                    lambda = 254.3, ic = "ebic")
fit
```

All the `ssj_*` functions return an object of class `ssj`, with `print` and
`plot` methods. The declared discontinuities reported above follow the rule of
the paper: an interval counts as a discontinuity when its estimated domain warp
$\hat\gamma_t$ clears both 5% of the total warping and 30% of the mean sampling
interval. The table itself is available through `ssj_breaks()`, which also
accepts a single absolute threshold through its `thresh` argument.

```{r}
ssj_breaks(fit)
```

The `plot` method reproduces Figure 4 of the paper: the fitted curve over the
data, with vertical lines at the declared breaks, and a lower panel with the
estimated warps, which measure the strength of each jump. The points shown are
the `r fit$nobs` distinct temperatures actually seen by the estimator rather
than all `r nrow(demand_temp)` observations. Pass `prob` to add a confidence
band, whenever the estimator returns pointwise variances (`ssj_mle()`,
`ssj_kfs()` and `ssj_fix()` do; `ssj_atw()` does not).

```{r fig.width=6, fig.height=6}
plot(fit, xlab = "Temperature (Celsius)", ylab = "Demand (MWh)")
```

All the declared breaks sit in the cooling region, between 27 and 30 degrees,
which is consistent with air conditioning being switched on once a comfort
threshold is crossed, and they are upward: demand rises abruptly. This is the
same reading as in the paper, whose Section 4.1 identifies the jump at 27
degrees as the most relevant one. A classical smoothing spline would round
these transitions off into a gentle curve. Lowering `ebic_xi` makes the search
penalty weaker and returns further, smaller breaks at low temperatures, where
electric heating plays a minor role in Italy.

The same data can be analysed with the CSSD algorithm of Storath and Weinmann
(2024), which penalises the number of discontinuities directly instead of a
warping budget. It is a different proposal, not one of ours, and the `print`
method says so.

Its `delta` argument is the pointwise noise standard deviation, and supplying
it is what makes the data-fit and roughness terms commensurate. Leaving
`delta = 1` on a series measured in MWh would make the data term dominate by
several orders of magnitude and return an essentially interpolating fit.

```{r}
# robust noise scale, immune to the jumps themselves
sig <- mad(diff(demand_temp$Load[order(demand_temp$Temperature)])) / sqrt(2)

fit_cssd <- ssj_cssd_potts(demand_temp$Load, demand_temp$Temperature,
                           p = 0.9, gamma = 10, delta = sig)
fit_cssd
```

`ssj_cssd_potts()` returns an `ssj` object too, so the same `print` and `plot`
methods apply. There is no lower panel here: CSSD has no domain warps to show,
because its discontinuity set is part of the solution of the underlying
combinatorial problem rather than a by-product of a continuous penalty.

```{r fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
plot(fit_cssd, xlab = "Temperature (Celsius)", ylab = "Demand (MWh)")
```

The fitted piecewise cubic spline can be evaluated at arbitrary temperatures
with `predict_cssd_potts()`, which is what makes the size of a discontinuity
directly readable:

```{r}
predict_cssd_potts(fit_cssd, xnew = c(20, 26.9, 27.1, 30))
```

The two methods are quite different -- one warps the domain under a budget
constraint, the other penalises the number of breaks directly -- yet both put a
discontinuity at about 27 degrees, which is reassuring.
